previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Crohn’s disease and multiple prior abdominal surgeries was admitted with abdominal pain and diarrhea consistent with a disease flare. Initial labs showed acute kidney injury, dehydration, and nongap metabolic acidosis, all secondary to fluid loss from diarrhea. CT imaging revealed fecal loading and mild stranding in the distal ileum, improved from prior studies, with no obstruction or hernia. He was treated with IV fluids, increased prednisone to 40 mg daily, and supportive care. His symptoms improved, labs normalized, and he tolerated a regular diet. Stool studies ruled out infection. He was discharged home on continued prednisone, a short course of pain medication, and instructions to follow up with gastroenterology.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ PMH ___ and nephrolithiasis recently discharged on ___ 
for treatment of Crohns flare presenting with worsening sharp 
and crampy abd pain and lower back pain and diarrhea. 

Active Issues:
# Abdominal Pain/Flank pain. 
The patient presented to the emergency department with diffuse 
abdominal and flank pain, accompanied by diarrhea. The patient 
stated that his pain was inconsistent with his previous ___ 
flares (the last of which he had been discharged for a week 
prior), but that it felt somewhat more like his prior kidney 
stones. His prior CT abdomen from his last admission did not 
show evidence of obstruction, and a renal ultrasound performed 
in the ED did not show evidence of obstruction.  The patient was 
admitted to the general medicine floor for further workup, and 
his pain was only partly responsive to pain medication. He was 
seen by GI and started on IV steroids; however, his normal ESR 
and CRP were not consistent with a ___ flare. A CT abdomen 
demonstrated no obstruction, and improvement of inflammation 
relative to his last admission, strongly suggesting against a 
renewed ___ flare. The patient was restarted on the 
prednisone taper with which he had last been discharged. 
Although the patient continued to have frequent loose stools, he 
stated that this was at his baseline. Prior to discharge, the 
patient tolerated clears and full liquids. However, he had 
considerable discomfort after attempting to start a regular 
diet, thus we recommended that he stay on a low residue diet for 
several days after discharge.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure to take care of you here at ___. You were 
admitted to the hospital for diarrhea and abdominal pain.  The 
most likely cause of your symptoms is gastroenteritis, an 
inflammation of your gastrointestinal tract, most likely due to 
a viral infection. Though these infections are uncomfortable, 
they are usually self-limited, and resolve without antibiotics.

During your stay you had an x-ray and a CT scan of your abdomen 
which did not demonstrate an obstruction and actually 
demonstrated improvement in your inflammation and there was no 
concern for Crohns flare. 

No changes have been made to your medication regimen.  You are 
still to take the prednisone you were given for your most recent 
___ flare, 40mg by mouth daily. You should continue this 
dosage 
until you see your gastroenterologist Dr. ___ will 
taper down your dose over time.

At this time, it was decided that you should return home to a 
soft, low-residue diet until your symptoms improve.  Should your 
pain increase, you should try waiting a brief period before 
eating again, and at that point begin with several meals of 
clear liquids (water, ginger ale, jello), before advancing to a 
diet of soft, low-residue foods. If you can only tolerate clear 
liquids for several meals in a row, contact your doctor.

If you begin to feel feverish, chills, or see blood in your 
stool or vomit, please contact your doctor or go directly to the 
nearest emergency room.
